title: Beyond Landau: When Symmetry Breaking Fails
description: The Quantum Hall effect as the prototype phase that no local order parameter can describe

concepts.title: The Landau Paradigm and Its Limits
concepts.contentHtml:
For most of the 20th century the Landau paradigm classified phases of matter by their symmetries: a phase is characterized by a local order parameter whose nonzero expectation value signals the breaking of some global symmetry. Magnetization breaks rotational symmetry in a ferromagnet; the BCS gap breaks U(1) charge in a superconductor; crystalline density breaks continuous translations in a solid. Distinct phases differ in the symmetry group of their ground state, and phase transitions are codified by the renormalization-group flow of an order-parameter field theory.

This works beautifully — until it doesn't. In 1980, Klaus von Klitzing measured the Hall conductance of a 2D electron gas in a strong magnetic field and found it quantized to one part in 10^9: σ_{xy} = ν e²/h with integer ν. No symmetry is broken between plateaus; the system looks identical microscopically across the transition. The Tsui-Stormer-Gossard 1982 experiment then found fractional values ν = 1/3, 2/5, 5/2, ..., ruling out simple band-structure explanations.

The Quantum Hall states are topological phases: distinguished not by any local order but by a global, topological invariant of the ground-state wavefunction. They have no Landau order parameter and no local distinguishing measurement. The 2016 Nobel Prize (Thouless, Haldane, Kosterlitz) finally recognized this revolution. Topological order forces a complete rethinking of what a 'phase of matter' even means.

concepts.title: Landau Levels and the IQHE Plateau
concepts.contentHtml:
Consider a 2D electron in a perpendicular magnetic field B. The single-particle Hamiltonian H = (p − eA)²/2m has spectrum E_n = ℏω_c(n + 1/2) with cyclotron frequency ω_c = eB/m. Each Landau level is massively degenerate: the number of states per unit area is n_B = eB/h = 1/(2πℓ_B²), where ℓ_B = √(ℏ/eB) is the magnetic length. The dimensionless filling factor ν = n_e/n_B counts how many Landau levels are filled.

When ν is an integer, the chemical potential sits in a gap between Landau levels. The bulk is incompressible — the only excitations cost finite energy ℏω_c — yet the boundary supports gapless chiral edge states, one per filled level, that propagate in a single direction set by B. These edge channels are protected: they cannot scatter backward without crossing the gapped bulk, so disorder is irrelevant to their conductance.

The Hall conductance plateau follows from this bulk-boundary correspondence. Each filled Landau level contributes e²/h to σ_{xy}; the longitudinal conductance σ_{xx} vanishes because there are no available bulk states to scatter into. The plateaus have astonishing precision because topology is robust: a small perturbation cannot change an integer. Indeed, the quantum Hall effect is now used to define the kilogram and ohm in the SI system since the 2019 redefinition.

concepts.title: Topological Order: A New Kind of Long-Range Structure
concepts.contentHtml:
Wen's notion of topological order generalizes the Quantum Hall pattern. A gapped phase has topological order if its ground-state degeneracy depends on the topology of the manifold it lives on (e.g., torus vs sphere) and cannot be lifted by any local perturbation. The fractional QH state at ν = 1/3 has a 3-fold ground-state degeneracy on the torus — this number is not encoded in any local observable; it is a global invariant.

Topologically ordered states host fractionalized excitations called anyons that carry a fraction of the electron's charge and obey statistics interpolating between bosons and fermions. They exhibit long-range entanglement — the ground state cannot be deformed to a product state by a finite-depth local unitary circuit. This is operationally distinct from the Landau picture, where every gapped phase with the same symmetry is locally equivalent.

Two complementary classifications now coexist. Symmetry-protected topological (SPT) phases (like topological insulators) have unique bulk ground states but protected boundary modes that survive only while the protecting symmetry is preserved. Intrinsic topological order (like fractional QH and Z₂ spin liquids) has no need for symmetry protection — the ground-state degeneracy and anyon content are robust under any local perturbation. Both lie outside Landau's framework, and together they organize the modern map of gapped quantum matter.

title: Integer & Fractional Quantum Hall: Chern Numbers and Laughlin
description: TKNN, the integer Chern invariant, Laughlin's variational wavefunction, and composite fermions

concepts.title: TKNN and the Chern Number
concepts.contentHtml:
Thouless, Kohmoto, Nightingale, and den Nijs (1982) gave the integer QHE its definitive topological reading. For a band insulator on a 2D Brillouin torus T², the Hall conductance is the integral of the Berry curvature Ω(k) over filled bands. The TKNN formula reads σ_{xy} = (e²/h) · C, where C is the first Chern number: an integer-valued topological invariant of the U(1) Berry connection.

The Berry connection A(k) = i⟨u_k|∇_k|u_k⟩ on the Bloch bundle plays the role of a U(1) gauge field over the Brillouin zone. Its curvature F = dA (or its non-abelian generalization for multiple bands) integrates to a quantized total flux: C = (1/2π) ∫_{BZ} F. Quantization is forced by single-valuedness of the Bloch wavefunction — this is the same argument as Dirac monopole charge quantization, transposed to momentum space.

Crucially, C is invariant under any continuous deformation of the Hamiltonian that doesn't close the gap. So σ_{xy} can only change by jumps when the bulk gap closes — a topological phase transition. This explains both the precision of the integer plateaus and the necessity of gap closings between them. Haldane's 1988 model showed that even without a uniform external B, a band insulator with broken time-reversal symmetry can have nonzero C — the first model of the now-celebrated quantum anomalous Hall effect, observed in 2013 in magnetically doped (Bi,Sb)₂Te₃ thin films.
mathExpressions: A_\mu(k) = i \langle u_k | \partial_{k_\mu} | u_k \rangle, \quad \Omega = \partial_{k_x} A_y - \partial_{k_y} A_x

concepts.title: Laughlin's Wavefunction and Fractional Charge
concepts.contentHtml:
The integer QHE is essentially a single-particle effect, but the fractional QHE at ν = 1/3 requires strong electron-electron correlations within the partially filled lowest Landau level. In 1983 Robert Laughlin proposed his celebrated variational wavefunction Ψ_{1/q}(z_1,...,z_N) = ∏_{i<j}(z_i − z_j)^q · exp(−Σ|z_i|²/4ℓ_B²), where z_j = x_j + iy_j and q = 3, 5, ... is odd to maintain fermion antisymmetry.

This wavefunction is remarkable for several reasons. It vanishes as the q-th power when any two electrons coincide, dramatically reducing Coulomb energy. It is an exact ground state of a short-range pseudopotential Hamiltonian. And — crucially — its quasi-hole excitations Ψ_qh ∝ ∏_i(z_i − w) Ψ_{1/q} carry charge e* = e/q: a fraction of the electron charge.

This fractional charge was experimentally confirmed by shot-noise measurements (de-Picciotto, Saminadayar 1997) showing tunneling current with quantum noise S = 2 e* I with e* = e/3. Even more strikingly, the quasi-particles obey fractional statistics: exchanging two quasi-holes multiplies the wavefunction by e^{iπ/q}, neither +1 (boson) nor −1 (fermion). They are anyons. Jain's composite-fermion picture organizes the entire principal sequence ν = p/(2mp ± 1) by attaching 2m flux quanta to each electron — the most accurate organizing scheme for the fractional QH plateaus seen in GaAs heterostructures.

concepts.title: Edge Theory and Bulk-Boundary Correspondence
concepts.contentHtml:
The boundary of a topological phase is not optional — it is mandated by the bulk topology. In the integer QHE with Chern number C, the edge supports exactly |C| chiral fermion modes, all moving in the same direction. Their dispersion is linear, so they form a 1+1D chiral Luttinger liquid. Backscattering is impossible without traversing the gapped bulk, giving them their celebrated robustness.

For the fractional QH state at ν = 1/q, the edge is described by a chiral boson φ(x,t) with action S = (q/4π)∫dxdt ∂_t φ ∂_x φ + .... Tunneling between two such edges across a constriction shows non-Fermi-liquid behavior: the I-V curve scales as I ∝ V^{2q−1} — a stringent test passed by experiments at ν = 1/3.

The bulk-boundary correspondence is now understood as a deep consequence of the Chern-Simons effective field theory S_{CS} = (k/4π)∫A∧dA, where k = 1/ν. The CS action is a topological term: under a gauge transformation, it produces a boundary term that must be canceled by gapless edge degrees of freedom — the anomaly inflow mechanism (Callan-Harvey 1985). The 2D bulk and the 1D edge form an anomaly-free composite. This pattern — bulk topological term plus edge anomaly — recurs throughout the modern classification of topological phases.

title: Anyons: Braiding Statistics and Fusion
description: Abelian and non-abelian anyons, fusion rules, and the Moore-Read state at ν=5/2

concepts.title: From Statistics to Braid Groups
concepts.contentHtml:
In 3D, exchanging two indistinguishable particles is governed by the symmetric group: the only one-dimensional representations are the trivial one (bosons) and the sign representation (fermions). In 2D, the topology of configuration space changes everything. The relevant object is the braid group B_n, generated by σ_i exchanging particles i and i+1 with the relations σ_i σ_{i+1} σ_i = σ_{i+1} σ_i σ_{i+1} (Yang-Baxter) but without σ_i² = 1.

This means an exchange in 2D is not equivalent to its inverse — going around clockwise vs counterclockwise are physically distinguishable. One-dimensional unitary representations of B_n are labeled by a phase e^{iθ} with arbitrary θ: these are abelian anyons, with θ = 0 bosons, θ = π fermions, and everything in between (including θ = π/q for Laughlin quasi-holes) physically realized in 2D quantum Hall systems.

The 2020 Manoharan-Bartolomei experiments and Heiblum's anyon collider results provided direct evidence of fractional braiding statistics in ν = 1/3 states. This is conceptually subtle: anyons are not new fundamental particles but emergent quasi-particle excitations of strongly-correlated 2D systems, whose statistics are protected by topology rather than by any underlying symmetry of the microscopic Hamiltonian.

concepts.title: Non-Abelian Anyons and the Moore-Read State
concepts.contentHtml:
When the Hilbert space of n well-separated anyons is multi-dimensional, the braid group acts via matrices rather than phases — exchanges are non-commutative, and the anyons are non-abelian. This degeneracy is not local: no measurement on any individual anyon can distinguish the states. The information lives globally, encoded in the topology of how the particles are braided.

The cleanest candidate for non-abelian statistics in nature is the Moore-Read Pfaffian state at ν = 5/2 in GaAs (1991). Its wavefunction is Ψ_{MR} = Pf(1/(z_i − z_j)) ∏_{i<j}(z_i − z_j)² · gaussian. Quasi-holes are predicted to be Ising anyons σ with charge e/4, fusion rule σ × σ = 1 + ψ, and quantum dimension √2. With 2N Ising anyons, the ground-state degeneracy grows as 2^{N−1}.

The ν = 5/2 plateau has been observed since 1987 (Willett), and 2018 Banerjee et al. measured its thermal Hall conductance κ_{xy} — a quantized signature of edge central charge. The result c = 5/2 was suggestive of the time-reversal-symmetric 'PH-Pfaffian' rather than the original Moore-Read or anti-Pfaffian, igniting an ongoing puzzle. Whether nature realizes Ising anyons here remains an open experimental question, but the theoretical framework is now central to topological quantum information.

concepts.title: Modular Tensor Categories: The Algebra of Anyons
concepts.contentHtml:
The mathematical structure of an anyon theory is a modular tensor category (MTC). The data: a finite list of anyon types {a, b, c, ...}, fusion rules a × b = Σ_c N_{ab}^c c (which channels appear when two anyons combine), and braiding/associator matrices R, F satisfying consistency conditions (the hexagon and pentagon equations).

The full content of an anyon theory is encoded in two matrices: the S-matrix encodes mutual braiding (the modular S transform of partition functions on the torus), and the T-matrix encodes self-statistics (twist eigenvalues θ_a = e^{2πi h_a} for each anyon). Their product satisfies (ST)³ = S²: the modular relations defining SL(2, ℤ). The total quantum dimension D = √(Σ_a d_a²) sets the topological entanglement entropy γ = log D, a measurable signature of topological order.

The smallest non-trivial anyon theories include the toric code (with anyons 1, e, m, ε = em, mutual statistics e^{iπ}), the Fibonacci theory (anyons 1, τ, fusion τ × τ = 1 + τ, golden-ratio quantum dimension φ), and the Ising theory above. Fibonacci anyons are particularly important: their braiding is universal for quantum computation — any unitary on n qubits can be approximated to arbitrary accuracy by Fibonacci anyon braids alone.

title: Topological Insulators and Z₂ Invariants
description: Time-reversal protected edges, Kane-Mele 2005, and the Bi-chalcogenide family

concepts.title: Time Reversal and Kramers Pairs
concepts.contentHtml:
An ordinary integer QH state requires breaking time-reversal symmetry (TRS) — the magnetic field is essential. In 2005 Kane and Mele asked: can a time-reversal-symmetric 2D insulator host topologically protected edge modes? Their answer was yes, and the relevant invariant is not ℤ but ℤ_2.

For spin-1/2 electrons, the time-reversal operator Θ = i σ_y K (with K complex conjugation) is antiunitary and satisfies Θ² = −1. Kramers' theorem guarantees that every eigenstate of a TRS Hamiltonian is at least doubly degenerate. At time-reversal invariant momenta (TRIM) k = −k mod G, the bands come in Kramers pairs.

This Kramers degeneracy is the seed of ℤ_2 topological protection. The way Kramers pairs of valence and conduction bands are connected across the Brillouin zone defines a topological invariant ν ∈ {0, 1}. ν = 0 is a trivial insulator; ν = 1 is a topological insulator. The Pfaffian formula (−1)^ν = ∏_{TRIM} √(det w(Λ))/Pf(w(Λ)) over the four 2D TRIM gives a computable expression in terms of the sewing matrix w_{mn}(k) = ⟨u_m(−k) | Θ | u_n(k)⟩.

concepts.title: Helical Edges and the QSH Effect
concepts.contentHtml:
The Kane-Mele 2005 model on the honeycomb lattice with intrinsic spin-orbit coupling realizes the quantum spin Hall (QSH) effect: a 2D ℤ_2 topological insulator. Its edge supports a helical pair of counter-propagating modes — spin-up moving right, spin-down moving left — locked together by TRS. Kramers' theorem forbids opening a gap as long as TRS is preserved.

QSH was first realized experimentally by König et al. (2007) in HgTe/CdTe quantum wells: above a critical thickness d_c ≈ 6.3 nm, the wells undergo a band inversion driven by spin-orbit coupling and become topological. Two-terminal conductance was observed to plateau at 2 e²/h — exactly the Landauer prediction for two ballistic helical edge channels — independent of sample width, as expected for a 1D edge state.

The 3D ℤ_2 generalization gives 3D topological insulators with gapless surface Dirac cones. The bismuth chalcogenides Bi₂Se₃, Bi₂Te₃, Sb₂Te₃ were predicted by Zhang et al. (2009) and confirmed by ARPES (Hsieh, Xia 2009). Bi₂Se₃ has a single Dirac cone at the Γ point with a bulk gap of about 0.3 eV — the largest of the family — and is the workhorse 3D TI material. The surface state is protected by TRS: nonmagnetic disorder cannot localize it, but magnetic doping or proximity gaps it open and produces axion-electrodynamics phenomena like the topological magnetoelectric effect.
mathExpressions: G = 2 e^2 / h \quad \text{(QSH two-terminal, helical edges)}
H_{\text{surf}}(k) = \hbar v_F \, (\sigma_x k_y - \sigma_y k_x) \quad \text{(Bi}_2\text{Se}_3 \text{ Dirac cone)}

concepts.title: The Periodic Table of Topological Insulators
concepts.contentHtml:
Kitaev (2009) and Schnyder-Ryu-Furusaki-Ludwig (2008) classified all gapped non-interacting fermionic Hamiltonians by their behavior under time reversal T, particle-hole C, and chiral S = TC symmetries. The result is the tenfold way: ten Altland-Zirnbauer symmetry classes, each with a periodic table of topological invariants depending on spatial dimension d.

The pattern has Bott periodicity 2 in d for the complex classes A, AIII and Bott periodicity 8 for the real classes (a manifestation of K-theory of K(R^d)). Class A in 2D gives the integer QHE (ℤ); class AII in 2D and 3D gives ℤ_2 topological insulators; class D in 1D gives Kitaev's Majorana wire; class DIII in 3D gives time-reversal-invariant topological superconductors like ³He-B.

Crystalline symmetries (point group, mirrors, glide planes) refine this classification dramatically. Topological crystalline insulators — predicted by Fu (2011) and observed in SnTe — are protected by mirror or rotation symmetry rather than TRS. The full landscape is now organized by topological quantum chemistry (Bradlyn et al. 2017): a database-scale framework that has, since 2019, identified topological band features in tens of thousands of real materials. With strong interactions, the non-interacting tenfold way breaks down: the ℤ classification of 1D class-BDI superconductors collapses to ℤ_8 (Fidkowski-Kitaev 2010), revealing that interactions can collapse, but never enrich, the non-interacting classification.
mathExpressions: T^2 = \pm 1, \quad C^2 = \pm 1, \quad S = TC \quad \Rightarrow \quad 10 \text{ AZ classes}

title: Topological Superconductors and Majorana Fermions
description: Kitaev's wire, Majorana zero modes, and the experimental hunt (2024 update)

concepts.title: The Kitaev Chain and Majorana Zero Modes
concepts.contentHtml:
Kitaev (2001) wrote down the simplest model of a 1D topological superconductor: a chain of spinless fermions with nearest-neighbor hopping t, p-wave pairing Δ, and chemical potential μ. H = Σ_j [−t(c_j† c_{j+1} + h.c.) − μ c_j† c_j + Δ(c_j c_{j+1} + h.c.)]. For |μ| < 2t with Δ ≠ 0, the chain is in a topological phase.

The trick is to decompose each complex fermion into two Majorana operators c_j = (γ_{j,A} + i γ_{j,B})/2 with γ² = 1 and γ† = γ. In the special point t = Δ, μ = 0, the Hamiltonian becomes H = it Σ_j γ_{j,B} γ_{j+1,A} — the bulk Majoranas pair up across bonds, but the two end Majoranas γ_{1,A} and γ_{N,B} are unpaired and commute with H. They are zero-energy edge modes.

Together, γ_{1,A} and γ_{N,B} form one nonlocal complex fermion f = (γ_{1,A} + i γ_{N,B})/2 whose occupation defines a 2-fold ground state degeneracy. This degeneracy is topologically protected: no local perturbation at one end can lift it, because the partner mode is at the other end. Nonlocal storage of quantum information is exactly the property one wants for fault-tolerant qubits.

concepts.title: Non-Abelian Statistics of Majoranas
concepts.contentHtml:
Majorana zero modes (MZMs) are Ising anyons: their fusion rule is γ × γ = 1 + ψ (an empty channel and a complex fermion), and their braiding generates non-trivial unitaries on the degenerate ground-state manifold. With 2N well-separated MZMs, the ground-state space has dimension 2^{N−1} — exactly N−1 'topological qubits' worth of nonlocal Hilbert space.

The braiding matrix for exchanging Majoranas γ_i and γ_j is U_{ij} = exp(π γ_i γ_j / 4). Two such exchanges square to −1, reflecting the spin-1/2-like character. Crucially, all braiding operations preserve γ_i γ_j-parity sectors but rotate basis states within sectors, giving a nontrivial Clifford-group action — sufficient for some quantum protocols, but not universal: Majorana braiding alone can only generate the Clifford group, requiring magic-state injection or exchange interactions to reach universality.

The most natural physical hosts are topological superconductors: vortices in a 2D px+ipy superconductor (and on the surface of a 3D TI proximity-coupled to an s-wave SC, per Fu-Kane 2008) bind one MZM each. Semiconductor nanowires with strong spin-orbit coupling, in proximity to an s-wave superconductor, in a Zeeman field — the celebrated Lutchyn-Sau-Das Sarma proposal (2010) — can also realize the Kitaev chain. The much simpler s-wave + spin-orbit + Zeeman recipe lit the global experimental race for Majorana modes.

concepts.title: Experimental Status (2024-2025)
concepts.contentHtml:
The history of Majorana experiments has been turbulent. Mourik et al. (2012) reported the first signatures — a zero-bias conductance peak in InSb/NbTiN nanowires. The peak survived as control parameters varied, fueling a decade of optimism. But subsequent work showed that trivial Andreev bound states can mimic exactly the same zero-bias peak signature, and several high-profile retractions (notably the 2018 Nature paper by Zhang et al., retracted 2021) prompted a major reckoning in the field.

Modern criteria are more stringent. The community now demands a quantized 2 e²/h zero-bias conductance plateau, demonstration of nonlocal correlation between two ends, and observation of the 4π-periodic Josephson effect. Aghaee et al. (Microsoft Quantum, 2023) reported passing the 'topological gap protocol' in InAs/Al heterostructures — necessary but not sufficient for MZMs. Microsoft's Majorana 1 chip, announced in February 2025, integrates eight topological qubits on a single device and aims to demonstrate fusion and braiding protocols on-chip; full peer-reviewed validation of qubit operation remained in progress as of 2025.

Alternative platforms continue to develop. Vortex MZMs in iron-based superconductors like FeTe_{0.55}Se_{0.45} (Wang 2018) and CsV₃Sb₅ (2023) have shown vortex-localized zero modes by STS. Magnetic atom chains on Pb (Yazdani group, ongoing). Planar Josephson junctions with InAs/Al (Fornieri 2019). The community is converging on the view that no single experiment will be definitive — instead, a coherent suite of measurements (transport, tunneling, interferometry, fusion) on the same device is required. The frontier of 2025 is precisely this multi-pronged demonstration.

title: Symmetry-Protected Topological Phases: AKLT and Haldane
description: SPT phases without topological order — the spin-1 Haldane chain as the prototype

concepts.title: Haldane's Conjecture and the Spin Chain Gap
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1983 Duncan Haldane made what was then a heretical claim: the spin-1 antiferromagnetic Heisenberg chain H = J Σ_i S_i · S_{i+1} with integer spin has a gapped ground state, while the half-integer-spin version (e.g., spin-1/2) is gapless. This contradicted the prevailing semiclassical wisdom that all 1D Heisenberg antiferromagnets should resemble the Bethe-ansatz spin-1/2 chain.

Haldane's argument used a nonlinear sigma-model description: the long-wavelength theory is the O(3) NLσM with topological theta term θ = 2π S. For integer S, θ ≡ 0 mod 2π and the theory is gapped (massive); for half-integer S, θ = π and the theory flows to a Wess-Zumino-Witten conformal fixed point that is gapless. The θ term distinguishes the two cases topologically — the difference is not in any local Hamiltonian property but in a topological term in the effective action.

The conjecture was confirmed experimentally in spin-1 chain materials such as Ni(C₂H₈N₂)₂NO₂ClO₄ (NENP) where the gap was directly measured by neutron scattering. The Haldane gap is now a textbook fact, but the deeper meaning was clarified only later: the spin-1 chain is not just gapped, it is in a symmetry-protected topological (SPT) phase — the simplest example in 1D.

concepts.title: AKLT and the Hidden Edge Spins
concepts.contentHtml:
Affleck, Kennedy, Lieb, and Tasaki (AKLT, 1987) constructed an exactly solvable point in the same phase: the spin-1 Hamiltonian H_{AKLT} = Σ_i [S_i · S_{i+1} + (1/3)(S_i · S_{i+1})²]. Its ground state has a remarkably simple description: split each spin-1 into two spin-1/2 components, form a singlet between adjacent components on neighboring sites, and symmetrize.

This valence-bond-solid (VBS) construction reveals the topological signature: on a chain of length L with open boundary conditions, the ends carry unpaired spin-1/2 degrees of freedom. The bulk is gapped and unique, but the edge supports a 4-fold degenerate manifold (one spin-1/2 per end) that is exactly degenerate as L → ∞. These edge spins were observed in NENP via ESR and in Y₂BaNiO₅ via NMR — the experimental fingerprint of a topological phase in a non-superconducting, time-reversal-symmetric magnet.

The matrix product state (MPS) representation of the AKLT ground state captures everything elegantly: the wavefunction is |Ψ⟩ = Σ tr[A^{s_1} A^{s_2} ⋯ A^{s_L}] |s_1 ... s_L⟩ with two-by-two matrices A^s built from Pauli matrices. The MPS bond dimension χ = 2 exposes precisely the spin-1/2 edge degree of freedom — this is the now-standard tensor-network way to detect 1D SPT order.
mathExpressions: |\Psi_{\text{AKLT}}\rangle = \sum_{s_1, \ldots, s_L} \mathrm{tr}\!\left[ A^{s_1} A^{s_2} \cdots A^{s_L} \right] |s_1 s_2 \cdots s_L\rangle

concepts.title: Classification: Group Cohomology and Beyond
concepts.contentHtml:
An SPT phase protected by symmetry group G is a gapped phase with a unique, symmetric, short-range entangled ground state, distinguishable from the trivial phase only when G is preserved. Break the symmetry and the phase becomes locally adiabatically connected to a product state.

Chen, Gu, Liu, and Wen (2011) gave a powerful classification: bosonic SPT phases in d spatial dimensions with onsite symmetry G are labeled by the group cohomology H^{d+1}(G, U(1)). The Haldane chain corresponds to H²(SO(3), U(1)) = ℤ_2, where the nontrivial element captures the edge projective representation — a spin-1/2 transforms projectively under SO(3), with R(2π) = −1 rather than +1. This projective-representation lens explains the edge spin cleanly: an integer spin in the bulk transforms linearly, but the edge carries a projective representation that is the topological invariant.

For fermionic SPTs, cobordism theory replaces group cohomology and gives a richer set of invariants — the modern framework uses generalized cohomology theories (Kitaev, Freed-Hopkins). The 3D fermionic topological insulator we met in the previous lesson is an SPT with G = U(1) ⋊ ℤ_2^T; its surface state's anomaly is captured by the bulk theta angle θ = π. This anomaly-inflow mechanism — the boundary anomaly that the bulk SPT precisely cancels — has become the unifying language: every SPT phase is labeled by the boundary anomaly it can host.
mathExpressions: \{\text{bosonic SPT in } d\text{D with sym } G\} = H^{d+1}(G, U(1))

title: Topological Quantum Computation: Braiding to Compute
description: Topological qubits, surface codes, and Microsoft's 2025 Majorana 1 announcement

concepts.title: Computing with Anyon Braids
concepts.contentHtml:
Kitaev (1997, published 2003) and Freedman-Larsen-Wang (2002) realized that non-abelian anyons could form the basis of a fault-tolerant quantum computer. The qubit Hilbert space is not the local state of any particle but the topological degeneracy of 2N anyons: 2^{N−1}-dimensional for Majoranas, exponentially growing in N for Fibonacci anyons.

Logical gates are implemented by braiding the anyons — physically dragging one around another in 2D spacetime. The unitary U_σ implementing each braid is determined entirely by topology: it is invariant under any continuous deformation of the path that doesn't cross another anyon. Local noise (a wiggle in the path, a stray photon) shifts the path but cannot change its topology, so it cannot affect U_σ. This is intrinsic fault tolerance at the hardware level — no quantum error correction needed for the gate itself.

The catch: which braids are achievable depends on which anyons you have. Ising / Majorana braids generate only the Clifford group — sufficient for stabilizer-circuit simulation but not universal (no T-gate, no quantum advantage). Fibonacci anyon braids are universal: any unitary can be approximated to ε error in O(log^c(1/ε)) braids by the Solovay-Kitaev theorem. So Ising-only schemes need supplementation by magic-state distillation or measurement-based tricks; Fibonacci-anyon hardware would be intrinsically universal but has no clear material realization yet.

concepts.title: Surface Codes vs Topological Qubits
concepts.contentHtml:
The dominant approach to fault-tolerant quantum computing today is the surface code, a stabilizer-code realization of toric-code ℤ_2 topological order on a 2D lattice of qubits. Logical information is stored in the topology of the lattice (boundaries, holes), and errors are detected by repeated measurements of plaquette and vertex stabilizers. Google's 2024 Willow chip demonstrated below-threshold scaling of a distance-7 surface code, with logical error rates dropping as the code grew — a major milestone toward fault tolerance.

The surface code is, in a sense, a simulated topological phase: native qubits are not anyons, but the encoded logical degrees of freedom transform like toric-code anyons under measurement-induced braiding. This requires a large overhead: each logical qubit at error rate 10^{−15} needs roughly 1000 physical qubits at 10^{−3} error rate.

A topological qubit built from Majoranas is a different paradigm: the protection is hardware-level rather than software-level. The hope is that fewer physical resources are needed because the gates themselves are topological, not just the storage. The catch is that the hardware must actually realize the topological phase, with all its decoherence channels (quasi-particle poisoning, finite-size splitting, thermal mixing) suppressed below the operating threshold. Whether the engineering of materials reaches this regime before software-based schemes win in raw qubit count is the central open question of the next decade in quantum computing.

concepts.title: Microsoft Majorana 1 and the 2025 Frontier
concepts.contentHtml:
Microsoft's Majorana 1 chip, unveiled February 2025, is the first integrated topological qubit processor. It uses an InAs nanowire / Al superconductor / hafnium oxide gate stack — a 'topoconductor' platform whose design follows a decade of Lutchyn-Sau-Das Sarma-style theory. Eight topological qubits sit on the chip, controllable via gate voltages and read out by interferometric quantum capacitance measurements.

The architecture is measurement-based: rather than physically braiding Majoranas (difficult in 1D wires), gates are effected by sequences of joint parity measurements on Majorana pairs — equivalent to braiding via the principle of measurement-only topological QC (Bonderson-Freedman-Nayak 2008). Single-shot readout of fermion parity has been demonstrated; demonstration of full braiding-equivalent unitaries on logical qubits was the announced near-term milestone, with full peer-reviewed validation still in progress through 2025.

The skepticism is sharp and substantive. The 2018 retraction reflexively conditioned the community to demand multiple independent signatures: not just zero-bias peaks, but quantized conductance plateaus, the 4π Josephson effect, nonlocal end-to-end correlations, and finally fusion/braiding statistics. Whether Majorana 1 clears all these bars is the open question of 2025-2027. Even if topological qubits ultimately fail to outpace surface codes on superconducting transmons, the deep lessons of topological phases — fault tolerance from topology, anyons as quasi-particles, anomaly-inflow boundary physics — have already permanently reshaped both quantum information theory and condensed matter. The next frontier is integrating these ideas with active research areas: fracton phases, non-invertible symmetries, and topological order in open (decohering) quantum systems.
